content: Auxilin, also known as putative tyrosine-protein phosphatase auxilin, is an enzyme encoded by the DNAJC6 gene in humans. The DNAJC6 gene is part of the DNAJ/HSP40 family of proteins, which are evolutionarily conserved and play a critical role in regulating molecular chaperone activity. This regulation is achieved by stimulating the ATPase activity of chaperone proteins. DNAJ proteins typically consist of up to three distinct structural domains. These include a highly conserved J domain, approximately 70 amino acids in length, which is usually located at the N-terminus of the protein. Additionally, they contain a glycine/phenylalanine (G/F)-rich region and a cysteine-rich domain. The cysteine-rich domain is characterized by four motifs that resemble a zinc-finger domain, as described by Ohtsuka and Hata in 2000. The structural organization of auxilin includes a protein tyrosine phosphatase domain and a C2 domain, both of which are located near the N-terminus of the polypeptide chain. Together, these domains form what is referred to as a superdomain, which is a tandem arrangement of two or more domains that are nominally unrelated but function as a single heritable unit. The phosphatase domain of auxilin is classified within the auxilin subfamily of lipid phosphatases. However, it is predicted to be catalytically inactive, meaning it likely does not exhibit enzymatic activity under normal physiological conditions.
